deep_dive.title: OCCAM: Improved Single-Cell Representation Learning and Perturbation Effect Prediction
deep_dive.abstract: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. We introduce Occam, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework for representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction. Occam combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It achieves the highest aggregate representation scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration. In cross-context few-shot prediction, a perturbation and a cell context are each observed during training, but never together. Occam better captures the measured response patterns for these unobserved combinations than four retrained competitors or direct transfer of the same perturbation's measured effects from other training cell lines. Without fine-tuning, Occam best distinguishes perturbations among the evaluated models and simple baselines in cell lines held out from predictor training, across seen and unseen assays. Predicting expression levels accurately in these settings remains challenging. For double perturbations, which target two genes simultaneously, Occam composes learned single-gene responses to better capture the combined response and reduce expression error compared with competing models and summed single-gene effects. These gains extend to both strongly additive and weakly additive responses. Together, these results support simple MLPs for cell representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction across contexts and gene combinations.

deep_dive.title: A Biologically Interpretable Single-Cell Pathology Foundation Model for Molecular Decoding of H&E Images
deep_dive.abstract: The microscopic structure of human tissues encodes molecular information that is not directly accessible by visual inspection. Current pathology foundation models improve histological interpretation but operate at multicellular resolution. It remains unclear whether routine histology contains structured molecular and cellular information recoverable at single-cell resolution, which biological properties are associated with this recoverability, and where its limits lie. Here, we introduce Loki2, a single-cell pathology foundation model trained on UniSeg, a pan-tissue resource integrating 15 million cells with segmentation, lineage annotations and measured or histology-inferred transcriptomic profiles. We examine the above question across cellular representation, molecular recoverability, and patient-level relevance. Loki2 captures cellular identity and continuous morphological variation, with interpretable latent dimensions linked to physical nuclear phenotypes through DAPI validation. Transcriptomic retrieval and in silico protein staining test molecular recoverability, with gene-level analyses revealing the strongest recovery for genes associated with morphologically distinct cellular identities and functions. Then, patient staging and biomarker discovery connect cellular morphology representations to clinical relevance. Together, these findings establish Loki2 as a biologically interpretable single-cell pathology foundation model and provide the opportunities of recovering cellular and molecular information from routine H&E histology at single-cell resolution.

deep_dive.title: Cell-state conditioning predicts the expression response to an unseen stimulus but not stimulus-dependent genetic effects
deep_dive.abstract: Second-generation sequence models can be conditioned on a cell state supplied as a single-cell snapshot rather than selected from a fixed catalogue, but whether that conditioning carries an experimentally applied perturbation has not been tested. We conditioned such a model on interferon-{beta}-stimulated and unstimulated monocytes from a published experiment, using cells disjoint from those providing the measurement, and asked whether the predicted expression response tracks the measured one and whether the same conditioning identifies expression QTL specific to the stimulated state. Predicted and measured responses agree at Spearman {rho} = 0.616 across 119 genes (95% CI 0.486 to 0.716), and at 0.607 after all 119 target genes are deleted from the conditioning input; across fifteen conditions the model's response scales with how much each condition's biology genuinely overlaps the target response (slope 0.73, Pearson 0.92), and a near-neighbour monocyte subset receives 0.295 against a measured overlap of 0.336. For stimulation-specific genetic effects we find no reliable evidence: the pre-specified primary arm moves from p = 0.0019 to 0.443 once both conditions must carry a measurable predicted effect, and the separation localises to the resting-condition baseline. Neither model generation's catalogue contains a perturbed sample, 0 of 4,430 tracks and 0 of 2,799 conditions, although both carry activation-state labels, so the gap is experimental perturbation rather than cell state. Two incidental findings apply beyond this model: credible-set membership mislabels over half of putatively condition-specific loci, and gating a ratio statistic on its larger term manufactures signal.

deep_dive.title: Averaging in gene perturbation benchmarks hides perturbation-strength variation: Consequences for model evaluation
deep_dive.abstract: Perturbation-response benchmarks usually represent each genetic intervention by averaging all cells assigned that perturbation label. We inquire what perturbation-strength information is lost by this averaging, and whether current model predictions preserve enough perturbation-specific information for this perturbation-strength variation to be evaluated. Using X-Atlas/Orion CRISPRi screens, we use depth-corrected guide abundance as a cell-level proxy for perturbation strength and examine how transcriptional responses vary within a nominal perturbation. Higher perturbation strength is associated with greater response reproducibility. The effect is present in two human cell lines, HCT116 and HEK293T, but is larger in HCT116. For model evaluation, HCT116 retrieval tests show that observed responses preserve perturbation identity, whereas the evaluated STATE and Cell2Sentence predictions do not reliably recover it, hence the question of within-perturbation strength information cannot be meaningfully evaluated.

deep_dive.title: Transferring CRISPRi knockdown responses to new cell lines requires screening part of each line
deep_dive.abstract: Perturb-seq screens measure knockdown responses in one cell line at a time. Models that transfer responses to new lines rarely beat simple averages, and standard metrics often ignore noise. It is unclear how much of a response is shared and what a new line must contribute. We studied CRISPR interference Perturb-seq of essential genes in four human cell lines, using noise ceilings and calibrated metrics. We also introduce CASTER, a set-based model that adapts the transferred mean to the target line. After noise correction, responses correlated at a median of 0.52, highest between the TP53 wild-type lines. With 30% of a line screened, a linear model and CASTER scored 0.84 and 0.80 versus 0.44 for the transferred mean (1 equals a technical duplicate). CASTER led only at 2.5% screened (0.62 versus 0.47) and fell below the transferred mean without a screen. Response size tracked general essentiality more than line-specific dependency.
deep_dive.llm_evidence_en: transferring Perturb-seq knockdown responses to new cell lines with a set-based model

deep_dive.llm_tldr_cn: Perturb-seq筛选每次只能在一个细胞系中测量敲低响应，而跨细胞系迁移模型往往难以胜过简单平均，且标准指标忽略噪声。作者在四个人类细胞系的必需基因CRISPRi数据上用噪声天花板与校准指标分析响应的共享程度，并提出集合模型CASTER将迁移均值适配到目标细胞系。结果显示噪声校正后响应中位相关为0.52，筛查30%细胞系后线性模型与CASTER显著优于迁移均值。
